newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Football listing to help kickstart Zambian bourse.
newsitem.headline: Football listing to help kickstart Zambian bourse.

text.p: Zambia's three-year-old stock market is forecasting dramatic growth in 1997 as more companies, including a football club, prepare to list and relative stability returns to financial markets.

The Lusaka Stock Exchange (LuSE) got off to a shaky start in 1994, worsened by a banking crisis the following year, but confidence returned last year and bourse officials and analysts are upbeat about 1997.
Turnover rose to $2.64 million in 1996 after dropping to $228,900 in 1995 from $368,384 in 1994.
"We expect the momentum to be maintained over the next 12 months," LuSE General Manager Charles Mate told Reuters.
Mate said public interest in the stock market should increase with the listing of Zambia Breweries and a football club, Mufulira Wanderers, later in the year.

Zambia Breweries is expected to be listed on the exchange on June 6. A total of 13 million shares are on offer at 150 kwacha (15 U.S. cents) under an offer closing next month. A date for the listing of Mufulira Wanderers has not yet been set.
"The listing of Mufulira Wanderers would be a very exciting innovation for the stock market," Mate said.
"We have tremendous enthusiasm for soccer in Zambia, and listing the team would both facilitate the flow of money to the capital market and enhance public understanding of how the market works.
"Zambia Breweries will fall in the same category because their products are well known," he added.
The exchange also expects BP Zambia, National Breweries and Metal Fabricators of Zambia (Zamefa), to have shares floated on the exchange before the year end.
"We are pushing the Zambia Privatisation Trust Fund to release BP, National Breweries and Zamefa, which have effectively been privatised," Mate said.

There are currently six companies listed on the Lusaka exchange -- Chilanga Cement, Farmers House, Rothmans, Trans Zambezi Industries (TZI), Zambia Sugar and Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines (ZCCM). TZI listed earlier this week.
"The market is likely to benefit from better valuations because of increased exposure. Analysts outside the country will be looking more closely at our market with the listing of TZI," he said.

TZI shares are listed on the Luxembourg stock exchange as the primary listing and were listed on the Zimbabwe stock exchange in February as a secondary listing. ZCCM shares are listed in both Paris and London.
The listing of such international companies would lend credibility to the market and encourage participation, Mate said.
Growing stability in the financial market would boost growth on the stock market, which contracted in 1995 when three commercial banks collapsed in the face of liquidity problems.
The yield on 28-day treasury bills has dropped from 108.5 percent in 1994, when the exchange was established, to below 30 percent, making investments in stocks increasingly attractive.
Interest rates on saving accounts, meanwhile, are down to between 15 and 20 percent from over 25 percent last year.
"We would be very pleased if the trend carried on to get interest rates below 20 percent," Mate said.
